title: An Arizona County’s “Housing Hub” Is a Dead End for Many Homeless Families
author: Zaydee Sanchez
content:
A decade ago, nonprofit leaders in Arizona’s most populous county boasted that
they had created the Amazon of homeless service systems. Families in crisis
would no longer have to contact a dozen agencies in search of shelter or
housing. A single system could point them to help.

But for all the hype, this system has become a dead end for many families. A
2023 evaluation found 94% of people who were assessed for housing help by the
system didn’t receive it. And that didn’t account for parents who were unable
to connect with a worker to see if they qualified for assistance.

Families say it hasn’t improved.

In interviews, 30 families that are homeless told ProPublica that calling the
hotline, meeting with outreach workers or showing up at shelters rarely
results in offers of help. Some families said they called 211 multiple times
without being connected to the homeless response system for families, known as
the Family Housing Hub. Others, who said they were sleeping in cars or
outdoors, said they couldn’t get a spot on the waitlist for shelter.

The system has returned to what it was a decade ago, with families calling as
many shelters as they can, repeating the very situation the hub was intended
to fix.

Those who did make it onto the hub’s waitlist said they were left guessing how
long it would take to get help. Some said operators told them to sleep in
their cars.

Vanessa Lopez said she experienced this frustration after leaving a hostile
relationship in the spring. While she and her two children stayed with a
friend, Lopez said she repeatedly contacted 211, which functions as a referral
service for the hub, hoping it would lead to shelter for her family.

Her friend eventually asked them to leave. Overwhelmed by the stress of not
knowing where to take her family, Lopez took a leave from her job. By then,
she said, she’d called 211 at least five times.

Yet no matter how dire her situation became, it still took months to get on
the waitlist for shelter. During one call she said she broke down in tears,
frustrated that others seemed to get help but she could not. She wondered if
she needed to be addicted to drugs to receive assistance.

“It’s not me telling you no,” she said the operator told her. “It’s the
system.”

Monique Lopez, the CEO of United Methodist Outreach Ministries, known as UMOM,
which runs the Family Housing Hub and the shelter waitlist, acknowledged the
frustrations of people like Vanessa Lopez (no relation). But before UMOM
offers callers shelter or a spot on the waitlist, the organization first tries
to help them find other options.

“We don't start the conversation with, ‘Hey, do you want to get on the shelter
waitlist?’” Monique Lopez said. “It really is ‘Let's try to figure your
situation out first.’”

Lopez attributed some frustrations to the number of organizations offering
assistance through the hub. Each shelter has its own rules, and some families
may not meet the requirements of every program.

To address the confusion, UMOM updated its website to provide more information
about the homeless response system for families, she said. The federally
funded system, known as Coordinated Entry, mandates that providers use an
assessment to prioritize scarce housing.

> “It’s not me telling you no. It’s the system.”
>
> 211 operator

But families told ProPublica that the process in Maricopa County often leaves
them confused and hopeless. Family homelessness in the county has risen to its
highest level in more than a decade, while every shelter is full and housing
vouchers are scarce. In 2025, there were [630
units](https://files.hudexchange.info/reports/published/CoC_HIC_CoC_AZ-502-2025_AZ_2025.pdf)
of shelter and transitional housing for families in the county, down from [769
the year
before](https://files.hudexchange.info/reports/published/CoC_HIC_CoC_AZ-502-2024_AZ_2024.pdf),
according to the most recent federal data.

Monique Lopez acknowledged that family shelters are full, leaving few good
options. “People are living in unsafe and unstable situations while waiting
just to get into emergency shelter,” she said.

The process, experts said, shouldn’t leave people wondering if there is help
and what it takes to get it.

“You have to have some kind of method for setting priorities when there aren’t
enough resources to go around,” said Marybeth Shinn, an expert on family
homelessness at Vanderbilt University. “The process should be transparent.
People should know if they’re on a waitlist.”

* * *

UMOM and other Maricopa County nonprofits launched [the Family Housing
Hub](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IvO0Om1zvJI) in 2014, after [years of
planning and strategizing](https://www.usich.gov/news-events/news/trust-and-
collaboration-drive-family-coordinated-entry-phoenix-arizona) over how to end
family homelessness in the county that is home to Phoenix. As they envisioned
it, families would meet with a worker at UMOM who could match them with the
best solution for their situation.

At the time, there was a national push to create these local systems. The U.S.
Department of Housing and Urban Development in 2012 asked communities to
establish a [Coordinated Entry
system](https://www.hudexchange.info/homelessness-assistance/coordinated-
entry/#coordinated-entry-notice). By 2018, the agency required it in order to
receive housing and homelessness grants. The mandates coincided with a Barack
Obama-era plan to end family homelessness by 2020. (That did not happen.)

Experts said the systems were set up without evidence they would be effective.
When researchers did look at Coordinated Entry — in a [2021
study](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/Qualitative-
Case-Study-of-the-Coordinated-Entry-for-All-System-in-King-County-WA.pdf) of
single adults — they found issues similar to those now faced by families in
Maricopa County, including concerns about fairness and a lack of transparency.
People didn’t understand the screening process and generally received vague
explanations about how their information would be used to decide if they would
get help.

As Maricopa County nonprofit leaders developed their system for families, they
also pledged to provide a “rapid response without waiting lists” to
immediately meet the needs of any family asking for help.

![A woman wearing a backpack sits at a picnic table under a gazebo while
several men and women wait in a line to be served food by two
volunteers.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/20260507-Sanchez-Family-
Homelessness-106.jpg?w=2560)People line up at what is known as “The Hill” in
Tempe, Arizona, to receive food from volunteers with the organization AZ Hugs,
which serves unhoused residents throughout the city.

The county saw a decline in family homelessness from 2015 to 2019. But then
the numbers began to rise, even as the stock of emergency shelter increased.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, efforts to address the problem began to fray.
The group of nonprofit leaders, which called itself “Standing Strong for
Families,” stopped meeting regularly. Arizona, along with other Sun Belt
states, also saw an increase in housing prices. With one of the [lowest
supplies of housing](https://nlihc.org/gap) for low-income people in the
country, [eviction filings began to
soar](https://www.kjzz.org/business/2025-01-06/there-were-87-197-maricopa-
county-evictions-in-2024-breaking-the-all-time-record-from-2005).

By 2023, only 6% of families that were assessed by Maricopa County’s homeless
response system received help with permanent housing, according to an analysis
of three years of enrollment data from the system and interviews with
providers and people who had sought housing assistance.

The evaluation, by Homebase, a nonprofit consulting group, was requested and
paid for by the Maricopa Association of Governments, which provides staffing
for the regional response to homelessness.

Homebase concluded the system for single adults who are homeless was
accessible, but the family system was not. Across the system, auditors said,
families encountered a “breakdown in communication” and a “lack of
transparency.”

Ashley Oakley, UMOM’s chief development officer, said in a statement that the
evaluation reflects a gap between the need in the community and the housing
that’s available. Oakley called it “one of the biggest challenges” facing
those who are working on family homelessness in Maricopa County.

To decide who gets onto the housing list, workers with the Family Housing Hub
conduct an assessment of vulnerability, which assigns a score based on how
long a person has been homeless and whether they have a disability. That score
helps determine eligibility and priority for housing programs, Oakley said.

Nonprofit leaders recently developed a new evaluation. Before it was
implemented over the summer, testing had showed it didn’t fully account for
the vulnerabilities of families and needed more changes. Now, for example,
households with children under 6 receive a higher score, making it more likely
they can get help.

Any family sleeping in a place not meant for “habitation” or in a dangerous
situation is eligible for shelter, said UMOM’s Oakley. To remain on the
shelter waitlist, families must check in weekly and say where they slept the
previous night. Staying in a hotel for a night should not “by itself” remove a
family from the waitlist, Oakley said.

But families told ProPublica that they had been removed from the waitlist
because they stayed in a hotel. (UMOM said it is reviewing its process to make
sure check-ins are handled “consistently.”)

Families in dire situations may not get help, said Richard Southee, a regional
executive director at Central Arizona Shelter Services, the largest shelter
provider in Arizona. Southee also works on a committee that oversees Maricopa
County’s response to homelessness.

That’s in part because the federal government has focused funding on more
noticeable forms of homelessness, such as people living in encampments.
Homeless families are typically less visible and move more frequently. They
couch surf, stay in hotels or do other things to avoid drawing the attention
of the Arizona Department of Child Safety. Child welfare officials sometimes
consider a lack of shelter to be evidence of child neglect, along with other
factors.

“We’re deciding who’s going to be at the back of the line, and we as a nation
really have said people who are not chronically homeless are going to be at
the back of the line,” Southee said. “You have to stay homeless to get to the
front, and that’s a design choice.”

Felicia Vela and her two children were kicked out of a guest house they were
renting in February, text messages from that time show. She said she searched
online for help and was repeatedly directed to 211 for “emergency shelter,”
which she called at least twice and explained her situation: She had stashed
her belongings in a storage unit, text messages show, and was staying at a
hotel that she couldn’t afford for much longer.

There was nothing immediately available, she said operators told her, with one
saying the waitlist was closed and the other telling her it could take six
months to a year to get shelter. (UMOM said to protect the privacy of clients,
it does not comment on individual families. The organization also said that
the waitlist does not close.)

When Vela didn’t have anywhere to go, she slept in her car while her children
stayed with a friend. She tried to make extra money by donating plasma, but
her blood pressure was too high.

Vela, who works a warehouse job, moved into an apartment with the help of a
local nonprofit that is not associated with the hub, but she’s now fallen
behind on rent and is facing eviction. Her car broke down, and she can’t get
to work. She started calling 211 again, seeking rental assistance.

“It’s like I can’t get a break,” she said.

* * *

Every January, volunteers in cities across the country spend one night trying
to count people who are homeless. In Maricopa County, the 2026 count showed
the number of people in homeless families, at 2,103, was the highest it had
been since 2015. The survey is considered an undercount, especially for
families.

Over the summer, the waitlist for shelter ballooned to more than 200 families.
It takes about seven weeks for those on the list to get shelter, according to
UMOM.

Some families interviewed by ProPublica said they waited longer. And more
people are entering the system than leaving it, delaying help for newly
homeless families.

In Maricopa County, 139 units of shelter for families closed from 2024 to
2025, after COVID-19 pandemic relief funds expired. The state also cut
$867,000 in funding to help families get into housing quickly. It had helped
about 40 families.

As families wait, they have searched for other ways to access the homeless
service system.

Some go to one of the city of Phoenix’s heat relief centers, inside a
21,000-square-foot former charter school. City officials said the number of
families seeking help has doubled from a year ago. Some families said they
were able to immediately get shelter through the workers there.

After city officials learned a local advocate, [Austin
Davis](https://www.propublica.org/article/arizona-homeless-austin-davis-az-
hugs), was sending families to the center to receive shelter, he said they
asked him to stop sending families.

Davis runs a local nonprofit that helps families like Vela’s find emergency
shelter. He said his interactions with hundreds of families over the past year
have shown the official channels to shelter are “too complicated.” Calling
weekly to stay on the waitlist is time-consuming. The families are already
managing day-to-day responsibilities while trying to resolve an overwhelming
personal crisis, he said.

“The system is really designed to run people in circles until they either give
up or hit enough roadblocks where they can’t continue,” Davis said.

Davis crowdsources donations to put the families in hotel rooms on and off for
days, weeks or sometimes months.

![A woman and young child hug each other while sitting on the bed in a hotel
room. Their hair obscures their faces, and the child is wearing
pajamas.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/20260507-Sanchez-Family-
Homelessness-136.jpg?w=2560)Ebony embraces her daughter inside the hotel room
where she was staying with five of her kids.

Ebony, a single mother of six who has breast cancer, needed longer-term help.
She lost her job as a security guard this year after a chemotherapy treatment
caused her to faint as she was about to begin her shift, she said.

In April, she lost her apartment. Ebony, who asked that her last name not be
used to protect future job opportunities, said she called every number she
could find looking for help, including 211. Eventually she was placed on the
waitlist, but that didn’t solve her immediate problem of where to sleep.

She and her children stayed in hotel rooms until she ran out of cash. Then,
she said, the family slept in an alley.

If a mother with breast cancer and young children sleeping outside was not
vulnerable enough to get help, she wondered, who was?

The next day, she connected with Davis, who helped her pay for weeks of
shelter. Then one morning she texted Davis with some good news.

She had met a pastor who helped her get into a local housing program. But she
needed help for a few more days, until she could move into her new apartment.
